The Distributional Impacts of Net-Zero Transitions · Submitted

with Hakkı Yazıcı


This paper studies the distributional consequences of net-zero transitions. Using an environmentally-extended input-output table linked with the U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey, we show that the carbon intensity of expenditure declines with income, largely due to differences in energy expenditure shares. We develop a heterogeneous agent overlapping-generations model with non-homothetic preferences, estimated using household-level data, that matches key distributional moments of the U.S. economy. We evaluate a carbon tax path consistent with the U.S. net-zero target under the Paris Agreement. Although the reform disproportionately affects poorer households in the short run, lifetime welfare costs are similar across income groups. Across cohorts, those in their fifties when the reform is introduced experience the largest losses. We find that the time path of carbon taxes impacts the distributional consequences of climate reforms substantially. An optimal reform that maximizes average welfare almost fully coincides with the carbon tax path implied by the Paris Agreement.

title: Public goods
text:
A few bits of code I’ve written over the years for fairly standard tasks that were annoying and time-consuming. I am confident in the accuracy of the code for my specific purposes, but no warranty whatsoever is offered for use elsewhere.

Data cleaning

Cleaning the Consumer Expenditure Survey

Stata code that cleans the CEX following Aguiar and Bils (2015). Handles top-coding, multi-quarter aggregation across the interview and diary surveys, and the 2013 redesign. Outputs a household-quarter panel with consistent expenditure categories from 1996 onward.


Cleaning the PSID

R code that cleans the PSID following Guvenen and Smith (2014). Constructs annual measures of earnings, wealth, and consumption with consistent definitions across the biennial waves post-1997.



Geography

Linking historical UK geographies

A Bash + Python pipeline that uses the ONS Geography Portal to crosswalk administrative geographies across boundary changes — parishes, wards, and LSOAs — with population-weighted apportionment for variables that don’t aggregate cleanly.
